title: Revolut Announces Launch of Dedicated AI Research Division: Revolut Research
summary:
Revolut, the global financial leader with over 80m retail customers, has today announced the launch of Revolut Research. Revolut Research is a dedicated division within the broader AI Department, established to pioneer next-generation machine learning architecture across global financial services. Set to build alongside leading academic and technology institutions, the unit provides a unified foundation for Revolut’s proprietary AI deployments and machine learning initiatives.
The global banking industry is hitting a technological wall as legacy institutions attempt to retrofit decades-old infrastructure with off-the-shelf software wrappers. This approach creates both soaring operational drag for organisations and leaves consumers with clunky applications and interfaces, and basic search-bar chatbots. Revolut is building differently, embedding native intelligence, developed in-house, directly into its core financial engine, turning local market data into a compounding global advantage.
Revolut Research serves as the engine behind PRAGMA, Revolut’s proprietary foundation model developed in collaboration with NVIDIA. Engineered specifically to decode complex financial behaviours and power real-time risk assessment, platform operations, and tailored product recommendations, Revolut is rebuilding its AI stack around a single foundation with one shared behavioural intelligence layer.
Head of Revolut Research, Anton Repushko, has already presented key findings at multiple high profile international conferences this year, including ICML in Seoul. Early deployments of PRAGMA on historical data have indicated major performance gains over legacy baselines:
Superior Credit Risk Accuracy: 2.3x higher accuracy at identifying credit default risk.
Smarter Fraud Prevention: 65% more fraud cases caught, with 17% greater precision in alerts.
Hyper-Personalisation: 41% more relevant product recommendations across retail and business accounts.
At the heart of this technical advantage is an unmatched global dataset. Serving 80 million customers across more than 40 markets, Revolut processes billions of cross-border transactions and diverse financial behaviours in real time. This data feeds into Revolut Research's models, creating a self-reinforcing loop and establishing a new language of financial behaviours. As the dataset grows, the models become exponentially smarter at detecting fraud, evaluating risk, and predicting user needs - creating a proprietary intelligence advantage that traditionally structured banks struggle to match.
"To lead the future of intelligent banking, you cannot rely on third-party blueprints," said Pavel Nesterov, Head of AI at Revolut. "We have launched Revolut Research to institutionalise our 'build, don't bolt on' philosophy. By training native foundation models on our global operational data, we are giving our engineering teams an unprecedented engine to deploy smarter features faster, eliminate systemic friction, and give our customers a safer, radically better financial experience."
“Revolut Research has been established to responsibly build financial intelligence at its deepest layer, rather than patching together narrow, specialised models," said Anton Repushko, Head of Revolut Research. "In PRAGMA, we are developing a single, unified foundation model capable of understanding the true nuance of financial behaviour in real time. Technology is in Revolut’s DNA, and by collaborating with global tech leaders, this division is engineering proprietary capabilities that set us apart from traditional banks.”
Beyond PRAGMA, Revolut’s advanced security models review nearly one billion transactions every month to stop fraudulent activity proactively, while connected engines power front-end capabilities such as AIR, Revolut’s in-app assistant that executes complex financial tasks in a single step (currently available in the UK only).
Looking ahead, Revolut Research plans to regularly publish its scientific findings and open-source technical frameworks. The Revolut Research team will also engage with the broader scientific community through international conferences, including NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October, ICAIF in November and will host quarterly meet-ups for the scientific community at Revolut’s offices.

title: Targeting 800+ Banking and Fintech Apps Across EMEA
summary:

Zimperium’s zLabs team identified 30 mobile malware families actively targeting more than 800 banking and fintech applications across 44 countries in the region.
The research shows significant concentrations of targeted applications in major financial markets, including the United Kingdom (72 apps), Spain (65), Italy (57), Turkey (56), Germany (55) and the United Arab Emirates (38).
Among the most active threats are TsarBot, CopyBara and Hook, which collectively target hundreds of banking applications using techniques including credential-stealing overlays, Accessibility Services abuse, screen recording and remote device takeover. Other malware families demonstrate a strong regional focus. For example, 90% of Nexus targets are concentrated in EMEA, while EventBot and MaliBot specifically target financial institutions in the region.
“Mobile banking fraud increasingly begins on the device, where attackers can manipulate the application experience, steal credentials and take control of legitimate banking sessions,” said Krishna Vishnubhotla at Zimperium. “The scale of targeting across EMEA shows that protecting the banking application alone is no longer enough. Financial institutions need visibility into both the application and the mobile environment where transactions occur.”
The findings come as financial regulators across EMEA increase scrutiny of application security, device integrity and digital operational resilience. Requirements and guidance including Europe’s DORA framework and measures from the Central Bank of the UAE reflect growing recognition that financial institutions must address risks originating directly on mobile devices.
Traditional security controls such as server-side monitoring, MFA and signature-based malware detection cannot address every threat occurring on the device. Zimperium helps financial institutions protect mobile banking applications through application hardening, runtime protection and AI-powered malware detection designed to identify and respond to threats directly within the mobile environment.

title: Payouts.com and Casper Association Partner on AI Agent Payments
summary:
Payouts.com, the financial operating system for humans and AI agents, and the Casper Association, the Swiss non-profit stewarding the Casper Network blockchain, today announced a partnership to bring x402 agent payments into production. Payouts.com will support Casper Network, the first WebAssembly-native Layer 1 running x402 on mainnet, as a settlement rail for its AgentWallet and Digital Employees platform. Since Payouts.com already supports x402 natively, the integration requires no protocol changes on either side.
AI agents are already doing real work: researching, negotiating, buying data, and calling paid APIs. As agents move beyond recommending actions to carrying them out and transacting, Gartner predicts that they could intermediate more than $15 trillion in B2B spend by 2028.  What they still mostly can't do is pay for any of it without a human holding a credit card. The x402 protocol changes that, turning HTTP's long-dormant "402 Payment Required" status code into a native payment step for machines.
Central to the execution is csprUSD, the Casper ecosystem's native stablecoin, designed as the standard settlement asset for agents transacting over Casper's x402 rails: stable, programmable, and enforceable on-chain, so an agent pays for an API call or a dataset in dollars rather than in a volatile asset. Payouts.com provides the governance control layer that governs what an agent may spend, on what, and when; Casper provides csprUSD-denominated settlement with on-chain enforcement, built for regulated and compliance-minded businesses.
Implementation is underway, with the integration rolling out in phases over the coming months. Details will follow through both companies' official channels.
Leor Ceder, CEO & Co-Founder, Payouts.com:​“The next wave of payment volume won't come from humans clicking checkout buttons, but from AI agents transacting on their behalf. Partnering with Casper gives our customers a settlement rail that is live today, not a roadmap item."
Michael Steuer, President & CTO, Casper Association:​ "Every era of the internet needed a payment layer before it could support real commerce. The browser got the credit card form. The smartphone got the in-app purchase. AI agents are the next buyers on the internet, and until now they've been transacting with borrowed human credentials. Payouts.com built the control layer for it; Casper built the settlement layer, with csprUSD as the currency agents actually transact in. Together, that's a complete stack for agent payments."

title: Large US Banks Move to Shield Consumers’ Passwords From Looming Quantum Threats – 1,500 Quantum-Resistant Cryptography Patents Filed Last Year
summary:
Banks and tech companies filed 1,455 patents for technology to prevent hackers to use quantum computing to intercept consumer’s bank transactions and steal their passwords in the year to 31 March 2026, shows new research by leading intellectual property law firm Mathys & Squire*.
 
It is expected that quantum computers will be able to crack many consumers' banking passwords, as they perform exponentially faster than today’s computers. Quantum computers will be able perform tasks in hours that would take today’s most powerful computers thousands of years.
 
Some experts believe quantum computers could be commercially available within the coming years, potentially enabling hackers to break into consumers’ bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets.
 
Bank of America (47 patents), Wells Fargo (44), JP Morgan (12) and Mastercard (9) are among the top patent filers of ‘quantum-resistant’ or ‘post-quantum’ cryptography technology. Many of the technologies filed are designed to prevent hackers from intercepting consumers' transactions and stealing their personal data.
 

Edd Cavanna, Partner at Mathys & Squire, says: “The looming threat of quantum computing is fuelling a race to develop and patent technologies that can protect consumers.”
 
“Developing quantum resistant technologies could give banks a significant edge over competitors. Quantum computing could make most of today’s security systems obsolete, and no real alternative has been found yet.”
 
“If robust security systems aren’t developed before quantum computers are rolled out, consumers’ savings would be exposed to criminals who could simply break into their bank accounts and take their money out.”
 
“This is not a remote risk. Some of the world’s largest banks and financial institutions are now involved in finding solutions.”
 
Edd Cavanna says cryptocurrencies are particularly vulnerable as they are built on traditional encryption methods that might not resist a quantum computing attack.
 
In the year to March 2026, 116 patents were filed for patents relating to protecting cryptocurrencies against quantum attacks, up 20% from 97 the previous year.
 
Examples of the ‘quantum-resistant’ technologies patented last year include:
 


A system that creates unique, randomised passwords for each financial transaction to be approved, reducing the risk of them being intercepted
A smart bank card that can update its own security software, allowing it to use better post-quantum technology as it becomes available
A centralised system allowing individual cryptocurrency holders to add multiple, changing layers of encryption to their crypto wallets
A system that uses AI to create different versions of people fingerprints for them to authorise transactions
* The research considers patent applications published between 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026

title: New Blackhawk Network (BHN) Research Finds Banking Access Shapes the Consumer Payout Experience
summary:
Blackhawk Network (BHN), a global leader in branded payments, today released new research* showing that while survey respondents expect fast access to business payouts, banking access significantly influences how they prefer to receive and use those funds. Business payouts are funds organizations distribute directly to individuals, including insurance and warranty claims, rebates, refunds, legal settlements, returned security deposits, incentives and other business disbursements.
Across all respondents, speed and immediate access emerged as shared priorities. Fifty-three percent of those surveyed said receiving their money quickly was important, while 45% said they valued being able to use funds right away. Beyond those common expectations, the research found meaningful differences in payment preferences, experiences with paper checks and the importance of digital wallet functionality.
“Organizations often focus on how quickly they can deliver payouts,” said Stacie Monjauze, Sr. Director, Business Development at BHN. "Our research shows that’s only part of the equation. Recipients have different needs based on how they access and manage their money, making flexibility and recipient choice important considerations when designing payout programs.”
Consumer payouts are used across a wide range of industries. As organizations continue growing these programs, the research suggests that understanding how recipients access and use funds can help create payout experiences that are faster, more flexible and better aligned with consumer needs. Among the findings:
Banking access shapes preferred payout method
Consumer preferences also differed in the types of payouts they wanted to receive. Across the consumer groups surveyed, cash-equivalent payouts and gift cards emerged as preferred payout options. Unbanked and underbanked consumers — those with no access or limited access to traditional banking — expressed stronger preferences across payout methods overall. These preferences reinforce the value of offering recipients greater flexibility and choice.
Digital access is part of the payout experience
The research also found that how recipients access and use funds after delivery matters. Forty-six percent of unbanked and underbanked respondents said the ability to add digital gift card funds to a digital wallet was very important, compared with 29% of fully banked consumers.
For many recipients, the payout experience does not end when funds are delivered. The ability to store and use funds digitally can be an important part of whether a payout is convenient and immediately usable.
Paper checks create greater friction for unbanked and underbanked consumers
Paper checks were one of the clearest examples of how banking access influences the payout experience. Nearly two-thirds (63%) of unbanked and underbanked consumers surveyed said they feel frustrated when receiving a paper check as a payout, compared with 46% of fully banked consumers.
The full report includes additional findings on payout preferences across different payment amounts, willingness to pay for faster access to funds, merchant credit, prepaid cards and gift cards, digital wallet functionality and other consumer payout behaviors.

title: Beyond Compliance: Why 58% of Europe’s Largest Banks Now Offer Premium APIs
summary:
Since PSD2, banks have been the primary providers of secure access to payment accounts. Today, the focus is moving toward what can be built on top of this — services that enable banks to generate new revenue and expand their role beyond traditional services.
Salt Edge’s latest report, Beyond compliance: premium APIs as a commercial opportunity for banks, explores how premium APIs help banks build on open banking foundations to support complex financial and treasury operations on commercial terms, often making banks invisible in daily workflows. 
The report outlines that banking is expected to fit directly into corporate processes, from SMEs that run daily operations through ERP platforms to end-users who need faster access to their bank accounts. Without deeper integrations and richer data capabilities, banks risk remaining disconnected from critical processes of firms, whilst clients continue to rely on manual operations and fragmented solutions.
Our analysis of the public developer portals at the 45 largest European banks reveals that 58% offer premium APIs, with several high-demand API product areas that address the needs of different customer segments:
Premium payment services (22 banks, 48.9%): Banks are extending payment capabilities with business-focused services such as treasury payment initiation, payment pre-validation, corporate refunds, payment collections, and commercial recurring payments. These APIs help companies automate payment operations, reduce processing friction, and gain greater control over financial workflows.
Premium account information services (14 banks, 31.1%): Enhanced account information capabilities provide businesses with deeper financial visibility through business account information, corporate account insights, and batch reporting. These services support more accurate financial analysis, reconciliation, and decision-making.
Beyond payment and account information services, banks are increasingly offering premium APIs in areas such as foreign exchange (13 banks, 28.9%), data verification and identity services (12 banks, 26.7%), loans and lease financing (10 banks, 22.2%) and more.
What’s behind Premium APIs
Regulation continues to provide the foundation for open banking, while leaving room for banks to develop services beyond mandatory requirements. As frameworks such as the proposed FiDA expand the scope of data sharing, premium APIs can build on this regulatory foundation to offer additional capabilities that are shaped by market demand and commercial priorities, with banks determining how these services are structured and priced.
Banks can tailor pricing to the use case and customer value, choosing pay-as-you-go for usage-driven services, subscriptions for recurring access, transaction-based fees for payment APIs, or revenue-sharing for services where banks participate in the value generated by their API. This allows banks to align API costs with usage while creating sustainable revenue streams.
Beyond open banking infrastructure
The challenge, however, is turning existing open banking infrastructure into a single, scalable API environment for both regulatory and commercial services, rather than maintaining separate layers.
This is where Salt Edge bridges the gap, with a single open finance platform that supports both regulatory and commercial APIs. Banks can extend their existing PSD2 infrastructure into premium services, avoiding a separate API stack and reducing development and operational costs. The platform connects banking services directly to corporate ERP and treasury systems using ISO 20022, enabling banks to embed payments, account data, and real-time events into existing business workflows without redirects or additional consent steps.

title: 87% of Finance Professionals Have Ignored Fraudulent Expenses, Reimbursements, or Claims, Medius’ New Financial Census Reveals
summary:
Medius, a leading provider of AP automation and spend management solutions, today released findings from its 2026 Financial Census, research from 2,386 finance executives across the US, UK, Sweden, and France. The headline findings reveal that workplace fraud is becoming normalized within finance departments despite heightened concerns about AI-generated scams.
The rise of the “shallowfake”
Eighty-seven percent of finance executives have ignored a small expense, reimbursement, or claim they believed was fraudulent. Meanwhile, 67% said they would be likely to engage in a minor dishonest expense claim themselves if the behavior were common among coworkers, fueling the rise of "shallowfakes" – low-value financial rule-bending, such as expense embellishment, adding up to significant business losses over time.
Nearly three-quarters (74%) of finance professionals believe small forms of fraud resulting in minor financial losses are already common in workplaces, while 64% said they would feel justified in committing a small dishonest financial act if they felt underpaid or undervalued. More than half (57%) admitted they would round up an expense or mileage claim if they believed it would go unnoticed.
At the same time, concern over AI-driven fraud is accelerating. Ninety-three percent of respondents said they are concerned about AI-generated fraud over the next 12 months. US organizations reported average yearly losses of $168,000 due to invoice fraud, with respondents seeing an average of one successful invoice fraud attempt per month.
“Costly deepfake fraud gets all the headlines,” said Chris Wilmot, Chief Financial Officer at Medius. “But while finance professionals keep a sharp eye out for these scams, hundreds of thousands of dollars are slipping out the back door through shallowfake fraud. These seemingly minor 'micro frauds' add up to death by a thousand cuts for organizations without the controls in place to catch them.”
Automation is here, so why are payments still late?
Despite 85% of finance teams reporting some level of accounts payable automation, nearly half of invoices still require manual intervention. Organizations estimate that 28% of invoices are paid late in a typical month, while 96% say managing late payments has contributed to stress or burnout among AP teams.
The impact of late payments extends well beyond finance teams. Nearly half (45%) of respondents said suppliers have imposed stricter upfront payment terms in response to late payments, while 43% reported suppliers ending relationships altogether. More than four in ten also said suppliers had reduced service quality or speed (42%) or escalated disputes to formal legal action (42%), highlighting the growing commercial consequences of delayed payments.
Kevin Permenter, Research Director - Financial Applications at IDC, comments: “Automation was supposed to make late payments the exception, not the norm. Yet the findings suggest many organizations continue to experience payment delays despite ongoing technology investment. As supplier terms tighten and business disruptions grow, the challenge is no longer simply adopting automation, but ensuring those investments deliver measurable operational outcomes.”
Finance teams are embracing AI – but they don’t trust it
AI adoption continues to accelerate across finance departments. Thirty-eight percent of finance executives already have agentic AI operating within at least some finance processes, while a further 50% plan to deploy agentic AI within the next 12 months. Despite this, trust remains a significant hurdle.
Ninety percent of finance professionals said there is always a financial or compliance threshold requiring human approval, regardless of AI accuracy or track record. At the same time, accountability for AI decision-making remains unclear. When asked who would be responsible if an AI error caused financial loss or a compliance issue, respondents were nearly evenly split between IT leaders, finance leaders, and the employees acting on AI recommendations. 45% of finance leaders said their teams often act on AI-generated recommendations without human intervention, highlighting the tension between growing reliance on AI and uncertainty around governance.
“Organizations are growing comfortable allowing AI to influence decisions, yet many still lack clear ownership when those decisions go wrong,” Ahmed Fessi, Chief Transformation & Information Officer at Medius, said. “As autonomous finance becomes more common, explainability, governance, and accountability are just as important as accuracy."
AI is reshaping who is hired, promoted and paid
The research also found that AI is increasingly influencing hiring and performance management decisions, shaping the next generation of finance professionals. More than half (55%) of finance leaders said AI fluency has become a meaningful differentiator in recruitment, while 86% said employees' use of AI is now a factor in performance evaluations.
Despite AI’s promises to relieve workers of menial tasks and make processes more efficient, AI is placing new pressures on finance teams. Three-quarters (75%) of respondents said AI usage has increased worker fatigue or burnout, underscoring the challenges organizations face as they adapt to rapidly changing expectations around technology, productivity, and skills development.
